Aurora Cannabis Shares Rally on Buyout Deal With Organigram, Fending Off Curaleaf Bid
Shares of Aurora Cannabis surged after the company accepted a C$561 million buyout offer from Organigram Global, securing a deal that thwarts a hostile takeover bid by rival Curaleaf Holdings.
Aurora's stock jumped 22.4% to C$7.21. Organigram shares fell 5.9% to C$1.28.

Under terms of the deal Aurora shareholders will receive C$7.80 per share, representing a 21% premium to Curaleaf's unsolicited approach and nearly double the stock's level before the takeover battle began in August. Aurora shareholders will have the option of being paid out in cash, stock or a combination of the two.
Foodtastic Makes Hostile Bid for Rival MTY Food After Being Rejected
Canadian restaurant franchisor Foodtastic launched a hostile bid for MTY Food valuing its rival at roughly C$982 million.
The parent of chains including Dunkin', Pita Pit, Quesada and Second Cup said Tuesday it was taking its offering directly to MTY's shareholders after being rebuffed.

News of the bid came shortly after MTY, which faces continued pressure from decreased consumer spending and a challenging operating environment, said it had parted ways with Chief Executive Eric Lefebvre.
MTY Food Names Victor Mandel as Its New Chief Executive
Shopify Squeezed by AI Compute Costs, Pre-Holiday Infrastructure Buildout
Shopify's third-quarter results and holiday guidance signaled mounting cost pressure from artificial-intelligence compute and infrastructure buildout costs.
Nasdaq-listed shares fell 8.7% to $142.57.

The ecommerce platform on Tuesday forecasted fourth-quarter gross profit growth to slip into the high twenties, trailing projected low-thirties revenue growth. The company expects operating expenses to rise to between 29% and 30% of revenue, while free cash flow margin is forecast to be roughly flat compared with the fourth quarter of last year.

The spread reflects the near-term cost of the company's push to embed generative AI directly into merchant workflows, as computing and token expenses for its Sidekick merchant assistant platform mount alongside elevated infrastructure costs ahead of the peak holiday shopping season.
Slowing Merchandise Sales Flash a Warning Sign
Thomson Reuters Quarterly Profit Falls After Year-Early Gain on Asset Sale
Thomson Reuters logged a drop in earnings in the third quarter after a year-ago boost from an asset sale and as it was squeezed by higher amortization of software.
Shares fell 9% to C$155.07.

The Canadian news and information provider said its net earnings fell to $339 million, or 78 cents a share, from $423 million, or 94 cents, a year earlier. The result last year was boosted by the sale of the company's remaining minority interest in the Elite legal financial management business.
Thomson Reuters 4Q Revenue Growth Expected to Slow
Fortis Lifts Dividend With Rise in Quarterly Earnings
Fortis bumped up its dividend payout after the Canadian utility logged stronger earnings on the back of rate base growth.

The holding company, which has electricity and natural gas operations in North America and the Caribbean, recorded third-quarter net earnings of C$545 million, or C$0.92 a share, against C$474, or C$0.81 a share, a year earlier.
On an adjusted basis, per-share earnings also rose to C$0.92, beating the C$0.88 mean estimate of analysts polled by FactSet.
Mercer International Expects to File for Bankruptcy
Mercer International expects to file for bankruptcy and plans to continue normal operations.

"With the support of the majority of our noteholders and shareholders, we are putting in place a much stronger balance sheet and the liquidity to navigate current pulp and lumber market and geopolitical conditions," Mercer said.
Mercer said about $1.1 billion of senior notes would be exchanged for equity, reducing existing senior note debt by about 88%.
Existing shareholders would receive about 8.5% of the new common stock and 3.5% of the new convertible preferred stock of the reorganized company.
TALKING POINT
Bank of Canada Gov. Macklem Pledges to Proceed Carefully on Further Rate Increases
By Paul Vieira
OTTAWA--Bank of Canada Gov. Tiff Macklem told the country's lawmakers that policymakers would proceed cautiously on delivering more rate increases due to elevated trade and geopolitical uncertainty.

During two hours before the federal legislature's finance committee, Macklem defended the decision to raise interest rates last week, saying officials needed to address a buildup of cost pressures and expectations that a larger share of firms would raise their prices over the next 12 months. Even with last week's quarter-point hike, the governor said rate policy would still provide support for an economy that's improving but not necessarily strong.
Macklem mostly reiterated the reasons behind last week's decision to raise interest rates: namely, a much higher inflation outlook driven by elevated energy prices and a modest improvement in growth.

The Bank of Canada increased its policy rate to 2.5% last week, marking the first boost in over three years. Macklem said there "could be a need to raise" rates further, while acknowledging that heightened levels of uncertainty continue to hover over the Canadian economy.
"Developments in the Middle East and Canada-U.S. trade relations both remain fluid," Macklem said.
"There is also uncertainty about the impact of new U.S. tariffs and how much energy costs will seep into consumer prices more broadly," he said.
However, he added, "we don't want to see higher inflation persisting."

Some economists, however, say they may revisit their outlook for rates following some weaker-than-expected indicators, most notably data measuring grossdomestic product. Employment data for October is out Friday, and a third-straight weak report could dial back market expectations for rate hikes, analysts say.

The Bank of Canada modestly upgraded its growth outlook for the economy, and in testimony Macklem cited an increase in exports, improvements in business investment, and evidence that firms are adapting to changes in the trade environment.

The economy, Macklem said, "is actually showing impressive resilience," and thereby no longer needs rate policy to be as accommodative. At 2.5%, the central bank's policy rate remains below the midpoint for neutral--the level at which interest rates neither contract nor stimulate economic activity. The Bank of Canada estimates the neutral rate in Canada is between 2.25% and 3.25%.
"What I would stress here is that at 2.5%, our policy rate is still not restraining growth. We've actually been supporting growth, but the economy doesn't need quite as much support," he said.
Some lawmakers questioned the need for a rate hike, with a member from the governing Liberals arguing this could dampen efforts by Prime Minister Mark Carney to increase business investment.

Macklem said there is ample evidence that a sizable share of firms intend to pass along their increased input costs to customers over the next 12 months. The central bank's official forecast has inflation over 3% for most of 2027, and returning gradually to its 2% target by mid-2028.
"We've got to do our best to look forward, to anticipate where the economy is going, and to use our interest rate to nudge inflation back to target," the governor said.
